extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance and standards for reporting accident, crime, death/funeral, weather, and sports news for newspapers — what to include in leads and bodies, sourcing, tone, and common pitfalls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weather story types and tone
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories of the weather belong in the accident division when they cause harm; weather stories vary from the pure accident type to the commonplace daily routine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When there has been severe atmospheric disturbance resulting in loss of life, destruction of property, or delayed traffic, a simple narrative of events is sufficient. For routine daily forecasts, value depends largely on the felicity of language; the reporter must exert himself to present the little-varying facts with originality because routine reports become monotonous. Examples: 'TERRIFIC STORM KILLS 4' vs. routine local forecasts. (New York World, Dec. 1, 1915; Indianapolis News, Oct. 28, 1913.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid sensationally 'playing up' causes
rubrics_metrics.description: Be cautious about emphasizing probable causes or promising developments beyond the facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text criticizes the 'shrewdness with which the reporter plays up the probable cause of the accident, adding to the actual facts and promising possible further developments in to-morrow's paper.' Reporters should avoid speculative embellishment and stick to facts or clearly attributed statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Death and funeral stories: tone (avoid bathos)
rubrics_metrics.description: In attempting to write sympathetically about the deceased, a reporter runs on the border line of bathos; it's easier to be ridiculous in such stories than in other news articles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most newspapers require reporters to confine themselves to bare statements of facts concerning the dead person's life rather than ornate eulogizing. Keep tone dignified and factual; avoid editorializing on the man's accomplishments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content of death stories (essential facts to include)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are a few facts which all death stories should contain: the person's name, age, street address, and position or business should normally be included in the lead, with possibly a statement of the cause of his death.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow-up facts may include duration of illness; names of surviving relatives and relationships with notable people; if married, marriage date and wife's maiden name and circumstances; length of residence in the city and birthplace; if wealthy, account of holdings and how acquired; close with pallbearers, time/place of funeral, minister officiating, and place of burial. Example illustration: the Justice Lamar obituary is cited as a dignified presentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obtaining information for death stories (sources and cautions)
rubrics_metrics.description: To gain information about a man who has just died, go first to the undertaker (for non-prominent persons); use county/state directories, city directory, old residents, close friends, and 'Who's Who' or morgue files for prominent persons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Caution against seeking details from family members unnecessarily. If using a morgue write-up, bridge naturally and easily between new and old material so readers do not suspect the story is partly written years ago. Example of poor coherence given (Pol Plancon item) to illustrate bad use of morgue material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crime lead: selectable features to emphasize
rubrics_metrics.description: In the lead to a crime story, one may feature either the names of the persons involved, the number of lives lost or endangered, the motive of the criminal, the nature of the crime, clues leading to identification and arrest, possible effects of the crime, or public sentiment resulting from the deed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Of possible leads, the names of the persons involved (criminal or victims) are most often played up. The text provides multiple sample leads showing different emphases (names, brutal nature, motive, etc.). Choose the feature that best serves news value and reader interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Body of the crime story: structure and content
rubrics_metrics.description: The body of the crime story follows the lead in a simple chronological narration of events, with interest added by quoting direct statements from persons immediately connected with the crime.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include descriptive details: how it feels to be held up, how the robber gained entrance, how bandits escaped. In burglaries and robberies, give value of stolen goods and any ingenious devices used. Unless purpose is obvious, give due emphasis to motive, but be on guard against accepting motives at face value. Investigate independently and draw your own conclusions rather than relying unquestioningly on police, detectives, or victims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution against libel and presumption of innocence
rubrics_metrics.description: Because of the strong temptation to make an accused person guilty before adjudication, reporters must be careful with wording and presentation of suspects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under American law, a person suspected or charged is innocent until proved guilty. Use cautionary phrasing: 'suspected of,' 'alleged to have,' or 'said by the police.' Provide the side of the supposed malefactor to present an unbiased story. Avoid appeals to readers' opinion; leave opinion to editorial writers. Historical examples (race riot in Atlanta, Leo M. Frank case) illustrate harm from sensational reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of slang on the sporting page
rubrics_metrics.description: In athletic stories reporters have almost complete freedom with language; slang is freely used because fans prioritize timeliness over style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Slang can brighten sporting stories and is acceptable to 'fans' provided every detail remains clear to them. The beginner must ensure clarity; slang is easily overdone and can choke a story with foggy jargon. Better no slang than a story cloyed with it. The author expresses hope sport pages will one day use purer English but acknowledges current practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of sporting news stories (four kinds)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sporting news stories fall into four kinds: (1) dealing with athletic events before their occurrence; (2) reporting the events; (3) analyzing and explaining the events and their results; and (4) dealing with the sport in general.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The second kind (reporting events) is similar to other news stories; the other three diverge and warrant separate handling. Choose approach and structure based on which kind the assignment is.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sports lead: priorities and typical features
rubrics_metrics.description: The lead to an athletic-event story often features the final result (score), with additional mention of causes of victory or defeat, equality/inequality of opposing players, and any important incidents; always include names of teams, time, and place.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because play-by-play is written as the game progresses, the lead is often written last to incorporate final results. If in doubt, feature the result. Examples given: short leads that emphasize the score, cause of victory, or individual contributions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Featuring names of teams and placement of the score
rubrics_metrics.description: Almost as frequent as the final score is featuring the names of the opposing teams, with the final score regularly included at the end of the lead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example format: 'Cornell, 24; Pennsylvania, 9' or leads that start with team names and close with the count.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feature cause of victory or defeat
rubrics_metrics.description: The cause of a team's victory or defeat often makes an effective feature for the lead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'With the aid of a bewildering assortment of plays, Syracuse defeated Oregon Agricultural College here to-day, 28 to 0.' Or: 'Inability to hit, coupled with poor fielding at critical moments, caused the defeat...' Use succinct causal phrasing to explain outcome.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feature individual players (praise or blame)
rubrics_metrics.description: Stellar work by individual players—or poor work when responsible for the loss—often justifies featuring their names.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Name key performers or those who made decisive errors; examples show naming pitchers, sluggers, or those who 'led an assault' and specifying contributions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Other sports lead/features: environment and crowd
rubrics_metrics.description: Other features that may be played up include the kind of weather, condition of the grounds, size of the crowd, and effect of the play on the crowd.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These contextual features can be effective hooks in leads and bodies (e.g., 'High winds and bad light made the marksmanship poor'; 'A disgusted crowd of 8,000...'). Include them when they materially affect the game or reader interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Body of sports story: length-dependent content and statistics
rubrics_metrics.description: The body may contain lineup, names of officials, mention of stars or poor performers, when and how scoring was made, condition of field and weather, and size of the crowd; longer accounts may give important plays chronologically or all plays for a detailed account.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If limited space, include a concise summary and boxed summarizing figures (attendance, receipts) and comparisons. For big events, papers often assign two men—one for a general account and another for detailed play-by-play. Include a regulation box score/lineup and standard statistical lines (errors, hits, stolen bases, double plays, left on base, bases on balls, strikeouts, umpires, time of game) as shown in the example baseball story.
